title: Inheritance and polymorphism
subtitle: Reuse a class, specialise it, and let one call do the right thing for every kind of object.

inh.title: Inheritance
inh.body: class Dog : public Animal makes Dog a specialisation of Animal: it inherits Animal’s members and may add or replace some. Use it for “is-a” relationships (a Dog is an Animal); use composition (a member object) for “has-a” (a Car has an Engine). Public inheritance is the usual form; private members of the base stay inaccessible to the derived class, protected ones are visible.

order.title: Constructor and destructor order
order.body: Creating a derived object runs the base constructor first, then the derived one; destruction is the reverse (derived destructor first, then base). The base part must exist before the derived part can rely on it.

over.title: Overriding and hiding
over.body: A derived class can redefine a base method. Without virtual the version chosen depends on the declared (static) type of the pointer or reference; with virtual it depends on the actual object type. Multiple inheritance (several bases) is allowed but can cause the diamond problem; virtual base classes solve it.

virt.title: Virtual functions and dynamic dispatch
virt.body: Declare the base method virtual and the call through a base pointer runs the override of the actual object. Internally each object with virtual functions carries a hidden pointer (vptr) to its class’s table (vtable) of function addresses; the call looks up the slot at run time.
virt.steps: Three objects in an Animal* array: Dog, Cat, Cow, each overriding speak(). One loop calling p[i]->speak() produces three different outputs — no if/else on type.

abs.title: Abstract classes and virtual destructors
abs.body: A pure virtual function (virtual double area() = 0;) has no body and makes the class abstract — it cannot be instantiated and acts as an interface that derived classes must implement. Always give a polymorphic base a virtual destructor, or delete through a base pointer skips the derived destructor and leaks.
abs.steps: Shapes: Circle r = 2 (π = 3.14), Rect 3 × 5. Areas via one loop over Shape*: 3.14·2² = 12.56 and 15; total 27.56.

rtti.title: Late binding cost and design tips
rtti.body: A virtual call costs one extra indirection and prevents inlining; it is negligible except in tight loops. Prefer small interfaces, favour composition over deep hierarchies, and mark overrides with override so the compiler catches signature mismatches.
